claims.text: Morwen is Sindarin for "Dark Maiden", from môr ("darkness, dark, night") + gwenn ("maiden").
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Silmarillion, "Appendix: Elements in Quenya and Sindarin Names", entries môr, wen

claims.text: Túrin was adopted by King Thingol, who sent messengers back to Hithlum bringing her news about Túrin's well-being, invitations from Thingol and gifts from Melian. But she refused to leave her home, not the least because her daughter Nienor was still a baby. In her stead she sent to Túrin the dragon-crested Helm of Hador, the heirloom of their house.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), Unfinished Tales, "Narn i Hîn Húrin (The Tale of the Children of Húrin)"; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Children of Húrin, "The Departure of Túrin"

claims.text: Morwen's house was oppressed by Brodda's Easterlings, although she received the help of Aerin, a kinswoman of Húrin whom Brodda had taken to wife against her will, and who knew Morwen's counsel. Meanwhile, Túrin had exiled himself out of Doriath and made himself a hero. The fame of the Black Sword reached to Hithlum, saying that he was cleansing Beleriand from perils, without Morwen knowing that he was her own son. Nienor now had grown up, and Morwen eventually fled the tyranny of Hithlum through Ered Wethrin and came to Doriath, only to find out that her son had left. Túrin's travels also brought him to the north and liberated Dor-Lómin, but it was too late, as Morwen and Nienor had long gone.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Children of Húrin, "The Return of Túrin to Dor-lómin"; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Children of Húrin, "Túrin in Nargothrond"

claims.text:
Morwen was then lost in the fog that arose from the Dragon's steamy breath and Mablung heard no news from her.
left|thumb|Húrin Finds Morwen by [[Ted Nasmith]]
Years later, Morwen, now in her fifties, came to the Forest of Brethil and found the graves of her children at Cabed Naeramarth. Húrin found her there. She was dying, and asked her husband how their son found his sister; but Húrin never replied. They spent the evening together until she passed away at sunset. Húrin dug for her a grave above Cabed Naeramarth on the west side of the Stone of the Hapless cutting the words Here lies also Morwen Eledhwen.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Silmarillion, "Quenta Silmarillion: Of Túrin Turambar"

claims.text: According to the words of Glirhuin, the mound survived the War of Wrath and as Tol Morwen was the westernmost isle off the coast of Lindon in the Second and Third Ages.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Silmarillion, "Quenta Silmarillion: Of the Ruin of Doriath"

claims.text:
Her epithet, Eledhwen, means "Elfsheen" or "Elven-fair". In the early Noldorin phase, it meant "Elf-maid". J.R.R. Tolkien mentioned that the Old English adjective aelfsciene had been applied to Sarah and Judith and translated this Old English adjective as "elven-fair".
She bore the title Lady of Dor-lómin, being the wife of Húrin, the Lord of Dor-lómin.
In early versions of the tale, she was called "Tirannë", "Mavwin", or "Mavoine".
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Silmarillion, "Quenta Silmarillion: Of the Ruin of Beleriand and the Fall of Fingolfin"; J.R.R.
